The integration of computer systems and economics has created a vast network of interconnected components, making program evaluation increasingly complex. This complexity is exacerbated by the difficulties in quantifying outcomes and implementing treatment assignments, which are further compounded by measurement errors and external validity concerns. Within this sophisticated ecosystem, economists have taken on a pivotal role in evaluating programs, drawing on a diverse range of methodologies to address these challenges. This paper seeks to provide a comprehensive geometric treatment of key econometric concepts, focusing on regression analysis, instrumental variables, and differential estimation. By employing a geometric approach, we aim to enhance our understanding of the underlying statistical principles and illustrate the derivation of desired estimates in a manner that is both visually engaging and mathematically rigorous. The geometric framework offers a novel perspective on the underlying issues, allowing us to visualize the relationship between true and estimated values, reconcile existing results, and establish a direct connection between linear regression and instrumental variables models. This revised perspective also paves the way for exploring more complex scenarios and deriving new results, opening up possibilities for future research.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of the conformal block diagram, specifically the region labeled as Clear Serre weights, utilizing the principles of p-adic Hukuhara-Kashiwata-Walther theory for the GL_2 case.

This study involves the development of a real-time damage indication system for composite materials through the use of electrical impedance tomography (EIT) and genetic programming. The material in question is a carbon-fiber epoxy laminate, and the indication method is designed to provide accurate damage information by analyzing changes in resistance within the composite. The calibration process for this system involves creating a computational model that generates a correlation between damage areas and resistance variations. However, due to the complexities of physical phenomena involved, an analytical model is employed to simulate resistance changes in a simplified manner. This simplified model is then utilized to develop a genetic algorithm that predicts damage areas based on resistance data from EIT scans. The effectiveness of this indication system is validated through a series of mechanical tensile tests on laminated composites with intentionally introduced defects. The results show that the system accurately identifies damage areas in composites with known defects. Furthermore, to simulate real-world applications, a notched composite sample is tested under varying mechanical stresses to create different damage scenarios. The outcomes indicate that the system provides reliable damage indication for both physical notches and naturally formed damage resulting from mechanical stress.

This work examines the connection between geometric measures and tensor representations of a Euclidean space within the context of differential geometry. A detailed exploration is conducted into how geometric measures such as the volume measure can be represented as tensors, focusing on a Euclidean space as the underlying manifold. A key aspect of the discussion involves deriving the expression for the Laplace-Beltrami operator in relation to the volume measure, with considerations given for both general geometric measures and specific measures such as the distance cube measure. The material presented is organized in a logical structure, beginning with fundamental concepts, before gradually building towards more complex analyses.

A right-angled Artin group (RAAG) is a type of group that has been gaining increasing attention, particularly in the fields of geometry, topology, and their interconnected areas. One of the key characteristics of an RAAG is that it can be defined by a simple graph, where the vertices represent generators and the absence of an edge between two vertices indicates a relation between the corresponding generators. In this context, we are concerned with the subgroups that split off during a recursive construction known as the "free splitting epimorphism sequence" induced by a graph's subgraph. We provide a comprehensive description of these subgroups for any RAAG mapped onto a surface group based on its underlying graph structure. Additionally, we explore how this information relates to other notable subgroups, such as parabolic subgroups, and we examine the intersection patterns between these subgroups. Our findings contribute to a broader picture of the structure of RAAGs and their implications for the study of their actions on various geometric spaces.

The development of fast iterative matrix inversion techniques has been a significant achievement, especially given the current surge in large-scale data processing. Our research extends these methods from low to high orders, ensuring they are suitable for use with partially permutated matrices, and further modifies them to be compatible with matrix blocks. We then implemented these advanced techniques on a GPU-enabled architecture and evaluated their performance. The results showed that higher order methods consistently outperform lower order variants, and that we can achieve significant performance gains by using higher order methods that take into account the standard deviation of the input data. Specifically, we found that a third-order method that considers the standard deviation of the input data data yields better results than a third-order method that assumes a unitary covariance matrix, and that it has a relatively lower computational complexity.

Contextual linear gambits is an extension of the gambit model that incorporates context information. A multi-agent setting with a central server that updates parameters based on local data has been proposed. In this setting, the context is not shared among agents, and a new approach called Federated Learning with Local Projections has been suggested. Theoretical guarantees indicate that convergence to an optimal strategy occurs when the context-space dimension is finite, or when the context set is compact and a regularity condition is met when the dimension is infinite. These results are valuable for designing context-dependent policies in areas such as economics and environmental management.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles form and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, hinder particle growth, it may also be stabilized by the same particles that form through growth processes. Evaluating the effects of particle development on VSI stability is crucial for understanding overall particulate distribution in these systems. Based on a stability model and theoretical predictions, conditions were identified under which VSI is suppressed or enhanced in different regions of the disk. In a situation where particles with a certain size range dominate, VSI is stabilized at higher altitudes and cooler temperatures on the outside of the disk, while an instance of instability occurs at lower altitudes and hotter temperatures on the inside of the disk. Conversely, when larger particles prevail, an instance of instability is seen on the outside of the disk at higher altitudes and cooler temperatures, while VSI is stabilized on the inside of the disk at lower altitudes and hotter temperatures. These findings suggest that particles formed through growth processes may seal off areas from VSI influence, leading to isolated, non-uniform patterns of turbulence and settlement behavior within the disk.

This paper establishes a Liouville theorem for a class of geometric structures known as Ricci diminutors, which consists of a metric component and a positive function component, and also proves a theorem on the dimension reduction of harmonic functions within this class, following previous work by Ashbach and Li for a specific type of structure where the curvature function is constant.

Recent advancements in vision transformers have led to successful applications in various tasks, ultimately generating great interest in localizing transformer components that excel in processing spatial information. This research seeks to further explore the utilization of positionals information in vision transformers, with a focus on the default position embedding scheme known as sinusoidal embeddings. A novel approach called Dynamic Entrances is proposed, where the position embedding scheme is dynamically updated based on the global average of the input data, thereby facilitating efficient spatial information processing. The proposed Dynamic Entrances framework was evaluated across multiple datasets, with vision transformer models outperforming their standard positionally-dependent counterparts in various benchmark tasks, with performance gains observed in nearly all assessments.

In the context of learning from diverse data for educational content, a challenge arises in ensuring student privacy. A three-player game can be utilized to achieve secure learning by dividing the data and updating models in an optimized way. Initially, a random stroll is taken through the data to estimate its distribution, after which a gradient-based update is applied to the model. A key aspect of this approach is a formula for updating the model linearly in response to the data it interacts with. A key contribution of this method is a closed-form update formula for the linear model in the presence of sensitive data. The optimal amount of data to use in the optimization process can be determined by calculating the variance of the data distribution. The fairness of the learning outcome can be assessed using the inequality of opportunity in grades. The method's effectiveness can be evaluated in terms of learning accuracy and the efficiency of the optimization process.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining a consistency objective with label noise, specifically designed to address this challenge. The proposed method excels in situations where there is a significant noise rate, has a strong foundation in theory, and demonstrates exceptional performance on publicly available datasets, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods.

In quantum mechanics, the phenomenon of steering enables one particle's state to be influenced by another's based on their shared history, despite a lack of direct connection between them. Previously, it was believed that entanglement was the sole cause of this phenomenon, leading to the definition of steering in terms of entanglement. However, recent studies have shown that single-particle entanglement can give rise to genuine nonlocal effects similar to steering, contradicting the initial assumption. A new definition of steering based on a particle's state being influenced by another's has been proposed, one that is not tied to entanglement. A new class of nonlocal effects has also been identified, one that is distinct from both steering and entanglement. A comprehensive understanding of these phenomena has been gained through the development of a multi-party steering monogamy inequality, one that is a direct consequence of a new regression inequality called the "hypercircular regression inequality." A clearer picture of quantum steering's underlying mechanics has been obtained, one that is valuable for utilizes of quantum effects in tasks such as secure communication and their manipulation in complex quantum systems.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth examination of Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, surveying current research, existing architectures, security and privacy threats, as well as challenges and potential solutions. Furthermore, the paper outlines a novel Blockchain-supported FL framework called 'CVaFL' that addresses issues with current implementations and meets the needs of IoVs data preservation. The contribution of this research is quantified in terms of multiple indices, demonstrating its superiority over competing approaches.

Deep learning models especially long short-term memory networks have been highly effective in various natural language processing and sequence data tasks but face significant challenges in their implementation for video identification due to the massive size of video data. This problem can be solved by designing both the model structure and hardware architecture concurrently. The paper presents a new design that combines both models and hardware to achieve more efficient video identification. A new model with fewer parameters was developed based on basic LSTM networks through a hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition technique. Additionally, a corresponding hardware architecture was designed that utilized a parallel processing method to reduce memory access latency. The results showed that the new model achieved better performance with reduced bit widths for weights and activations compared to state-of-the-art models. The designed hardware architecture was also found to improve performance by 2.3 times over a high-performance GPU. The research provides a foundation for future applications in image recognition, where substantial size differences exist between images and videos.

A prime decomposition in a free group F can be viewed as a product of fundamental commutators, and previous research has established that applying a homeomorphism to each fundamental group F0 through Fn0 will result in a homeomorphism for the product group F0...Fn0. In this study, we demonstrate that this homeomorphism property persists when considering iterated compositions of functions, specifically those that map the product group back to the unit cube. Our findings involve constructing a homeomorphism for the product group F0...Fn0 by applying a composition of homeomorphisms within each fundamental group F0 through Fn0, and we further develop a theory to analyze the behavior of these compositions at the level of fundamental groups.

This study investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a nonlinear interaction force, with a focus on scenarios where the initial energy is positively infinite, and the potential force meets certain conditions. A key finding is that despite the potentially infinite initial energy, solutions remain bounded and converge over time, with the exception of a specific instance where a blow-up occurs within a specific time frame. A key contribution is the derivation of global existence results, with multiple instances of it being found under varying scenarios, including cases where the potential force is harmonic, log-harmonic, or satisfies a specific boundary condition, among others. Additionally, it is found that in scenarios where the global existence result is achieved, steady-state solutions that are homogeneous in space are the only solutions that remain positive over time.
We provide a detailed explanation for establishing semi-parametric local uniform deductions of varieties over positively characteristic algebras that are finitely generated from $\mathbb{Q}$.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. While Bayes factors provide an effective tool for theory testing, their practical use is often hindered by the challenge of accurately estimating model probabilities, particularly when dealing with complex models and limited data. This challenge is particularly pronounced when attempting to establish a hierarchy of theories, as it demands a Bayes factor that quantifies overall hypothesis preference. In response to this challenge, we explore alternative approaches that prioritize the estimation of Bayes factors over model probabilities, focusing on a Bayesian framework that utilizes bridge sampling. The paper introduces a meta-analysis technique that integrates the estimation of Bayes factors across multiple studies, as well as a method for deriving a scaling factor that stabilizes Bayes factor estimates and enhances their negative log approximation. Furthermore, we present a code repository that provides an implementation of the described strategies, along with an analysis of a published cognitive science study to demonstrate their effectiveness.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate how discourse indicators convey sentence relations, which is the primary focus of this paper. Existing studies have established that discourse indicators impact sentence interpretation, but more information is needed on exactly how they convey meaning. To achieve this, the research utilizes predicted indicators to annotate discourse indicators used in existing linguistic datasets, which describe their semantic implications. These findings serve as the foundation for creating a new dataset, termed DiscSense, which is publicly available for use in future research.

We derive a one-parameter group of Jordanian twists by applying our previously established construction method. This approach involves using a one-parameter group of differential operators that act on the underlying vector space, specifically a one-parameter group of conformal transformations. We utilize this one-parameter group of conformal transformations to define a new one-parameter group of Jordanian twists, which meets the requirement of being time-dependent.

This study formulates an extended differential dynamic logic that integrates with first-order logic and utilizes the Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives. A new proof procedure is also developed, combining the Brzozowski's derivatives with the Brzynowski differential inclusion. Theoretical contributions include the Brzozowski's derivative operators for the regular expression languages that match the extended KLE, the closure properties of the Brzozowski's derivative languages, and the soundness of the proof procedure. The most significant contribution is the implementation of an automated solver called "RegExDiag" that utilizes the developed framework, specifically the Brzozowski's derivative operators, the Brzynowski differential inclusion, and the universal property of left quotients, to resolve extended regular expression inequalities.

Building upon previous work by Ferrara, Furlano, Grillo and Miele, we have derived a new representation of spinning operator product expansion segments in CFT$_2$ by taking their perspective as boundary operators in AdS$_3$ CFT. We have also obtained a Poisson summation formula analogous to one established by Fitzpatrick, Kaplan and Manohar for general use with spinning operators.

To greatly increase the sensing area of a broad-field X-ray monitor employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a multi-focal-plane approach where multiple LE lenses are used, each focusing X-rays at a different point in the detector. By utilizing this configuration, a much larger field of view can be covered with a fixed-sized detector. Specifically, our calculations indicate that with a 10m² detector, we can effectively observe a field of view of 1 steradian, with an energy resolution of ~1000, when utilizing this multi-focal-plane approach with three LE lenses.

The large-scale structure of the universe can be predicted using cosmological simulations, which typically account for gravity's effect on matter through the Poisson equation. However, when observing the universe, we measure the distribution of light from stars, which only indirectly indicates the mass of objects. Consequently, predicting the mass of dark matter halos around these objects is a complex task that researchers face. To address this challenge, a new approach using deep learning techniques has been proposed, specifically a neural network called 'halofactory', which incorporates an analysis of the velocity field of the universe. Initially, this method appears to improve prediction accuracy; however, further analysis reveals that the velocity field information is actually redundant. To confirm this discovery, a new simulation was conducted, ignoring the velocity field effects on the initial conditions, which resulted in velocity field-independent predictions. These findings suggest that the velocity field's influence on the halo mass prediction derives from its correlation with large-scale structure, which can be represented through the linear density field. Consequently, using a neural network that incorporates the velocity field offers no significant advantage over existing approaches that consider the linear density field.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak magnetic fields. As a response to this challenge, researchers have turned to atomic interferometry, which offers a sensitive method for detecting magnetic field changes. Typically, long atomic Compton wavelengths are advantageous for this purpose, but they also limit the usefulness of this technique in strong magnetic fields where their behavior becomes complicated. On the other hand, using short atomic Compton wavelengths can provide more stability, but it requires more complex experimental setups. In this research, we exploited the distinct behavior of superconducting materials in repelling magnetic fields, known as the Meissner effect, to create a simple and stable environment for atomic interferometry. By positioning a superconducting material near the atomic beam, we could eliminate the influence of strong external magnetic fields and achieve extremely high sensitivity in measuring weak local magnetic fields. Ultimately, we achieved a sensitivity of 10^-12 teslas, which surpasses the limits set by the Bloch-Siegert shift and the AC Stark effect, and also approaches the theoretical optimum of 1.3 x 10^-12 teslas for Rb atoms.

A comprehensive quantum theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spin configurations of magnetic adatoms and their combinations on non-magnetic substrates. This model takes into account the overlap between adjacent adatom wave functions, which is particularly important for understanding the formation of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states in close-packed arrangements. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the theory was applied to a single manganese adatom and a manganese dimer on a niobium substrate, with its predictions validated through its consistency with existing knowledge. The results obtained were also graphically represented for easier visualization.

This report details our methods and results as we competed in a challenge to develop an effective system for detecting skin cancer using images.  A three-layer CNN was initially employed to extract features from images, which were then classified using a threshold value.  However, this approach yielded disappointing accuracy.  To improve performance, we incorporated entropy values derived from image regions to distinguish between healthy and abnormal pixels, which significantly enhanced the feature maps produced by the CNN.  By using these enhanced feature maps to train a new CNN, our team achieved a challenge-winning accuracy of 93.3% for detecting skin cancer.  Our success suggests that entropy could be useful in developing systems for detecting unusual samples in image classification tasks.

Due to the tendency for high-energy collisions to produce vector bosons in their earliest stages of development, accurately estimating their production rates is crucial. In the context of future colliders such as a 100-TeV muon collider, predicting these rates is particularly important, given its potential to surpass existing energy records. A key challenge arises when attempting to determine the production rates of vector bosons, specifically W and Z, in the aftermath of hadronic events. This problem can be framed as a statistical estimation task, where a large amount of background data competes with a relatively small amount of signal data. This study investigates various methods for addressing this challenge, incorporating both theoretical knowledge and real-world data from the LHC. Ultimately, the most effective approach is found to utilize a combination of existing theoretical information and machine learning techniques, specifically a neural network-based method that produces accurate estimates of W production rates with a mere 1% of available data.

We bring together Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser in a single paper and provide a complete translation of their little-known 1933 Polish discussion on the incompleteness theorems, as well as a detailed analysis of their arguments. We also include a biographical sketch of Leon Ostrovici, who played a significant role in their meeting, and a concise overview of their key contributions to logic, all written in an engaging and accessible style.

This article examines the concept of invariant sets within dynamical systems, specifically in relation to a surface that persists unchanged after a system's transformation. A fundamental theorem in classical dynamical systems states that an invariant closed set, that is not a subset of the system's equilibrium points, will either be an equilibrium state itself or form the basis for a topological manifold consisting of multiple isolated invariant circles/cycles around a hyperbolic equilibrium point. However, this theorem is not directly applicable to fractional-order dynamical systems due to their unique characteristics. Such systems may exhibit novel dynamics and have been shown in previous studies to possess invariant closed curves around a hyperbolic equilibrium point in certain situations. Therefore, the authors sought to investigate if invariant two-dimensional manifolds could exist within these systems following a planar reaction-diffusion model. The study's findings indicate that in most cases, no such invariant surfaces exist within these fractional-order dynamical systems.

This study reverses the conventional structural acoustic model where an unknown acoustic signal is estimated based on measurement data of a structure's vibration. Instead, we aim to reconstruct the structure's vibration state when the vibration data is known but the acoustic excitation is unknown. A key challenge in solving this reversed problem is that it involves inverting both linear systems described by partial differential equations. We meet this challenge by utilizing the observability operator from the linearized infinite-dimensional model, then using interpolation techniques to handle structural-acoustic coupling variability. We treat each possible note played on the instrument as a distinct instance with its own variability model. By combining the reconstructed vibration data with an acoustic simulation, we can further determine the instrument's note being played. This reversed structure-acoustic image reconstruction technique has numerous applications in noise source identification and music instrument research.

Within the most fundamental scoto-seesaw framework, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, dark matter phenomena, and the stability of the vacuum state. By implementing a natural $U(1)_{\rm D}$ gauge symmetry breaking process, we derive a spectrum of fermion masses that meets the required conditions. Utilizing one-loop renormalization group equations, we evaluate the stability of the vacuum state and the consistency of the model by ensuring the weak gauge boson non-remotalization. Additionally, we analyze the dark sector's dynamics, incorporating the one-loop threshold corrections to the dark photon mass, and examine the constraints imposed on the model parameters. We further investigate the possible dark nucleon-nucleon interaction modes and the corresponding limits on the parameter values. Employing the numerical solution of the two-body recoilless electron spin lattice relaxation phenomenon, we calculate the dark photon decay constant and examine the dark matter relic abundance. Utilizing the one-loop effective potential, we evaluate the $U(1)_{\rm D}$ gauge boson mass and confirm its consistency with the dark sector's dynamics. Finally, we examine the possible dark matter relic abundance scenarios and the corresponding constraints on the parameter values.
